responses.title: Try a smaller step first
responses.body: A big change in taste is hard to keep. A smaller reduction often sticks better, and you can step down again later.

responses.title: Give your taste a week to adjust
responses.body: Taste for sweetness usually adapts with a couple of weeks of consistent change. If it still feels too different, your dietitian can agree a gentler step.

action.reason: Patient finds the agreed sweetness reduction hard to accept; consider a gentler interim step.

responses.title: Make it automatic
responses.body: Plan the exact words before you reach the counter, and link the request to something you always do.
responses.script: When I reach the drinks stall, I'll say: "{{option}}, thank you."

responses.title: Keep a planned exception
responses.body: One planned usual drink a week can make the other days easier. Choose the day in advance so it doesn't feel like a slip.

action.reason: Patient asks for one planned exception day a week to support adherence.

responses.title: A change you can say for yourself
responses.body: When someone orders for the group, a short phrase said in advance keeps your change without making a fuss.

responses.title: Choose a change you control on your own
responses.body: Drinks are ordered one by one, so they're easier to change than shared dishes. Keep your drink change and leave shared food as it is for now.

responses.title: Pick a change that doesn't depend on the stall
responses.body: If your usual stall can't adjust sweetness, a change that works at any stall keeps you on track.

responses.title: Have a back-up stall
responses.body: Note a second drinks stall nearby that can make your order, so a closed stall doesn't break the week.

responses.title: Make the order quicker than the old one
responses.body: Choosing a drink that needs no adjustment avoids the extra step when you're short of time.
